readerTitle: The 'For Sale' sign: buy a business or start your own?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 주방용품 가게, 요가 스튜디오용 예약 소프트웨어) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 사업을 사는 값에서 물건값을 뺀 웃돈은 '검증'의 가격이다. 그 검증이 판 사람이 떠난 뒤에도 남는지가 핵심이다.
misconception: 직접 시작하는 게 훨씬 싸다. 또는 수익이 검증된 사업을 사면 그 수익도 그대로 따라온다.

sources.text: 소규모 사업 인수의 일반 개념 (영업권, 실사, 판매자 분할 지급·인수인계)

factChecks.note: 가게: 인수가 $300,000 − 집기·재고 등 실물 $120,000 = 웃돈 $180,000. 인수가 ÷ 연 수익 $90,000 = 약 3.3년. 모두 가상 수치입니다.
소프트웨어: 400개 스튜디오 × 월 $30 = 월 $12,000, 연 $144,000. 인수 요청가 $360,000 = 연매출의 2.5배. 가상 수치입니다.
7번 카드의 대금 일부 후불·인수인계 조건은 일반적 관행으로만 서술했고, 특정 국가의 법률·세무 조언은 하지 않습니다. 표현을 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: The 'For Sale' sign in the shop window
body: Walk down almost any main street and you'll see one: a small shop with a handwritten sign. *Business for sale. Ask inside.*
Behind that sign is a choice every would-be owner faces. Build your own from nothing, or pay more to take over one that already works.

image.label: A small shop window with a handwritten 'Business for sale' sign
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 동네 상점가의 작은 가게 유리창에 손글씨 "Business for sale · Ask inside" 종이가 붙어 있고, 안에는 손님 두어 명과 계산대 뒤 나이 든 주인. 옆 가게는 비어 있고 "For lease" 표시. 실제 브랜드·로고 없음.

cards.title: Start a shop or buy one?
body: You want to run a neighborhood kitchenware shop. Starting your own costs about $120,000 for fit-out and stock, with no customers yet.
The shop down the street is for sale at $300,000. It has paid its owner about $90,000 a year for several years. Which is the better deal?

options.text: Start fresh. It costs less than half as much
options.feedback: You save $180,000 in cash, but you pay in months of building customers, with no proof it will ever earn $90,000.

options.text: Buy. At $90,000 a year, it pays for itself in about 3 years
options.feedback: That math only holds if the $90,000 keeps coming after the owner leaves. That's the part you haven't checked yet.

options.text: It depends on how much of the $90,000 would stay without the current owner
options.feedback: This is the real question. The extra price only makes sense if the business keeps working once it's yours.

cards.title: What the extra $180,000 buys

breakdown.label: Physical stuff
breakdown.detail: Fixtures, stock, equipment you could buy anyway

breakdown.label: The premium
breakdown.detail: Customers, staff, supplier terms, a lease, years of records

cards.callout: That premium is often called **goodwill**: the price of a business that already works. Starting costs less cash. Buying costs less time and guesswork.

cards.title: Buying vs starting
body: When you **start**, you pay with time and risk. You spend months finding customers, hiring and learning what sells, with no guarantee it works.
When you **buy**, you pay cash to skip that stage. The premium is a price for proof.
So the question isn't which path is cheaper. It's whether the proof you're paying for will still be there after you take over.

image.label: Two paths: a long winding road labeled Start and a short toll bridge labeled Buy
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Start" 길은 길고 구불구불하며 "Find customers", "Hire", "Learn what sells" 표지판이 있음. 오른쪽 "Buy" 길은 짧은 다리인데 입구에 "Premium" 요금소. 두 길 모두 같은 가게로 도착.

cards.title: Part of the premium can walk out the door.
body: Ask where the $90,000 comes from. Walk-in customers who like the location and the range will likely stay with the shop.
Customers who come because they've known the owner for 20 years may not. The same goes for a supplier deal built on a personal friendship.
If half the earnings depend on the owner, you're paying a proven-business price for half a proven business. The more that stays with the shop, the more the premium is worth.

cards.title: The same trade shows up everywhere.
body: Buying is common wherever winning customers is slow:
list: An accountant buys a retiring accountant's client list
A cleaning company buys a rival's office contracts
A plumber takes over a retiring plumber's van and phone number
A developer buys a small app that already has paying users
cards.callout: In each case, you pay to skip the slowest part: finding customers who trust you.

cards.title: The seller knows more than you do.
body: The owner has lived through every bad month. You've seen a few spreadsheets. A lease ending next year, a big customer about to leave, or a slow decline can hide inside good-looking averages.

Check several years of records, read the lease, and talk to customers and suppliers. Many buyers also ask the seller to stay for a handover or take part of the price later, so the seller shares the risk. Get local professional advice on the deal itself.

cards.title: Now it's software.
body: You're a developer who wants a small software business. A founder is selling a booking tool for yoga studios: 400 studios pay $30 a month, about $144,000 a year. The asking price is $360,000.
The founder answers every support email personally. Building your own version would take you most of a year. What do you do?

options.text: Buy now. The revenue is already proven
options.feedback: Proven for this founder. If studios stay because of the founder's personal support, some may cancel once they leave.

options.text: Build your own. It's far cheaper in cash
options.feedback: You keep the $360,000, but you spend a year with no users and still have to win 400 studios from scratch.

options.text: Check the churn trend and why studios stay, then tie part of the price to customers staying
options.feedback: You pay for proof only after testing it, and the seller shares the risk if users leave with them.

cards.title: Starting costs time. Buying costs a premium for proof.
body: Before paying that premium, ask how much of what works will keep working without the seller.
**Try it today:** pick a business you know well. List what would stay if the owner left tomorrow, and what would leave with them.
